summary.text: 太 is a marked form of 大, with a dot distinguishing the graph. It is associated with ‘great’ and ‘big’ as well as degree meanings such as ‘very’ and ‘excessive’; the dot is a graphic marker, not an established picture or sound cue.

formation.text: Indicative: 太 is formed by adding a distinguishing dot to 大. This describes the graph’s differentiation; the dot is not shown to contribute a separate meaning or sound. The proposed picture of a person added for scale and a phonosemantic analysis are unsupported by the cited paleographic account.

components.text: 大 is the base graph in this differentiating form. It is associated with ‘big’ or ‘great’; its contribution here is not evidence that 太 developed through a single semantic path from 大.
丶 is the added visible dot. It distinguishes 太 from 大; no independent object, meaning, or sound function is established for it.

history.text: The curated comparison is a modern seal-script-style rendering of 大, not an ancient form of 太. The paleographic account identifies distinguishable 太 forms in Western Han inscriptions, including 太初, while treating proposed earlier examples as disputed or reading them otherwise; it does not supply a complete sequence of forms.
Before 太 became graphically distinct, pre-Qin texts used 大 for words later written 太. The history of that graphic distinction is separate from the history of the spoken words.

uncertainties.text: The graphic analysis supports a distinguishing dot, but does not establish that it depicts a person or supplies a sound. Individual occurrences of 大 require contextual interpretation, and the relationship among ‘big’, ‘great’, ‘very’ and ‘too’ is not a securely ordered semantic chain.
The Western Han dates and readings are reported through the paleographic account; no dated primary artifact image was inspected for this entry. Some alleged pre-Han 太 forms remain disputed.

senses.text: 太 is associated with ‘great’ and ‘big’. Earlier texts often wrote 大 for words later written 太, so the meaning of any particular 大 occurrence depends on its context.

太 is used as a degree word meaning ‘very’ or ‘much’. Interpretations of excavated texts report degree uses written with 大, and sometimes 泰, before 太 became a distinct graph; this does not establish one linear semantic development.
The sense ‘too’ or ‘excessive’ is reported both for 太 and in interpretations of early degree-word uses written 大. The evidence does not securely order it relative to ‘very’ or ‘great’.

limitations.text: The evidence supports overlapping associations with ‘great’, ‘very’ and ‘excessive’, but not a dated chain or priority among them. The reported earliest distinguishable graph is Western Han; that does not date the word’s earliest use.

overview.text: 太 marks 大 with a dot to distinguish the graph. It commonly means ‘very’ or ‘too’ and is also associated with ‘great’; the dot is a graphic marker, not an established picture or sound cue.

evidence.source: 陳家寧, “說‘大’、‘太’和‘天’的關係,” Fudan University Center for Excavated Texts and Paleography
evidence.text: The author argues that 太 is a differentiating form based on 大, with one or two dots added as a distinguishing mark. The earliest distinguishable 太 forms identified in the article are Western Han: an inscription on a palace vessel of Emperor Wu’s era has 太初; the article also cites an inscription from two years later. Earlier bronze, Qin, and early Western Han examples in titles and words later written 太 use 大. The article says pre-Qin texts originally used 大 for words later written 太, and Han transmission could have replaced 大 with 太; it cautions that each occurrence of 大 requires contextual interpretation. It also rejects some proposed earlier 太 forms as uncertain or misread, including a Zhou pottery form it reads as a 大夫 ligature and an oracle-bone personal name whose reading is unresolved.
evidence.title: 陳家寧：說“大”、“太”和“天”的關係

evidence.source: 陳家寧, “說‘大’、‘太’和‘天’的關係,” Fudan University Center for Excavated Texts and Paleography
evidence.field: sound and meaning relation; ancient use; semantic cautions
evidence.text: The author reports that 大 and 太 were close in sound and meaning, with differentiation possibly involving an initial consonant contrast; the article gives traditional Middle Chinese categories for 大 and 太 and discusses later dialect evidence. It cites pre-Qin textual variants and bronze usage where 大 corresponds to later 太 in titles and compounds. This supports overlap and later differentiation, but does not by itself establish a single linear semantic path from ‘big’ to ‘very/too’; occurrence meanings need contextual interpretation. The article also treats 大 and 天 as historically related, but that is a separate relation and does not establish 太’s graphic origin beyond its derivation from 大.
evidence.title: 陳家寧：說“大”、“太”和“天”的關係

evidence.field: dated degree-adverb uses in excavated sources
evidence.text: The article distinguishes the degree-adverb word from the graph used to write it. It interprets Western Zhou oracle-bone and bronze examples of 大 as degree intensification, including forms it reads as excessive degree, and reports that this word was ordinarily written 大 or sometimes 泰 in excavated materials through the Eastern Han. It cites Warring States and Qin-Han manuscripts such as Guodian Laozi, Shuihudi, Mawangdui and Zhangjiashan. These are the author’s readings and semantic classifications, not a simple graphic chronology.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The accessible sources do not establish any semantic or phonetic role for the added dot. The strongest inspected analysis treats it as a graphic differentiator, so the dossier’s phonetic-compound and ‘normal-sized man for scale’ explanations are not supported by this evidence.

No directly dated primary inscription image was visually inspected. Dates and readings of the cited Western Han vessel inscriptions are reported through the paleographic article, not independently verified here.

The semantic history from 大 ‘big’ to 太 ‘very/too/much’ is not fully established by a dated sequence of lexical attestations in the inspected sources. The article reports pre-Qin spellings with 大 and contextual later 太 readings, while explicitly requiring case-by-case interpretation.
No original-object, loanword, or phonetic-component borrowing claim is supported or investigated as necessary: the inspected account explains 太 as graphic differentiation of 大.
Official Unicode Unihan endpoint access failed. The local Unihan row and Baxter–Sagart row were supplied in the prompt and were not independently inspected; do not cite them as externally verified.
No inspected primary artifact photograph independently verifies the article’s readings or dates for the Western Han 太初 vessel inscriptions.

The accessible evidence does not establish a unique linear semantic path from ‘big’ to ‘very/too’; excavated sources preserve overlapping uses and the specialist authors caution that manuscript dating and later transmitted-text spellings complicate chronology.

The exact origin and function of the dot are not independently demonstrated beyond its analysis as a distinguishing graphic mark; neither a person-for-scale account nor a phonetic role for 丶 is supported.
The identity and reading of several alleged pre-Han 太 forms remain disputed in the paleographic account; no image assets for those candidates were selected.
No reliable image of a dated 太 form with verified identity and reuse provenance was established. The selected comparison asset shows 大 only; it is a modern redrawing, not an ancient artifact image.

The official Unihan record endpoints for U+5927 and U+592A returned internal errors; current readings here are attributed to the supplied local rows. Local Baxter–Sagart rows were also supplied rather than independently inspected.
The Shuowen passage discussed by Chen concerns 大/亣 and 泰; it does not directly document the dotted 太 graph.
The inspected evidence does not establish graph borrowing or a depicted tool/object name underlying 太.
